The reported outcome is the specific assay characterization of IS20 and IS21.

title: Deep-learning virtual screening finds antibacterial hits in over one billion compounds
summary: Genentech and collaborators trained the deep-learning model GNEprop on high-throughput screening data and screened more than 1.4 billion synthetically accessible molecules. In follow-up experiments, 82 selected compounds showed antibacterial activity against the sensitized E. coli ΔtolC strain; the paper reports a 90-fold higher hit rate than the training screen and describes chemically diverse hits, some with activity beyond that strain and validated biological targets.
ai_technology: GNEprop deep-learning antibacterial activity predictor
organization: Genentech Research and Early Development; NVIDIA; Mila–Université de Montréal collaborators

evidence.tested: In follow-up experiments, 82 selected compounds showed antibacterial activity against the sensitized E. coli ΔtolC strain; the paper reports a 90-fold higher hit rate than the training screen and describes chemically diverse hits, some with activity beyond that strain and validated biological targets.
evidence.unknown: The 82 confirmed hits were tested for single-dose activity against the sensitized E. coli ΔtolC screening strain; this is not evidence that all 82 work against wild-type bacteria or in infections. The 90-fold improvement refers to hit rate relative to the HTS training experiment. Some additional compounds were selected for dose-response testing; do not imply all virtual hits were validated. A publisher correction fixed a coauthor’s misspelled first name and did not change results.
evidence.ai_role: GNEprop was trained on approximately two million small molecules screened against E. coli ΔtolC and used to rank a much larger synthetically accessible library for experimental prioritization. The follow-up assays confirmed antibacterial activity for 82 compounds; biological characterization also investigated specific targets.

title: Prospective machine-learning screen identifies six previously unreported OATP1B1 inhibitors
summary: Researchers trained and compared seven machine-learning classifiers for OATP1B1 transporter inhibition. In prospective CHO-cell testing, 15 of 19 compounds predicted active by SVC models inhibited the transporter; six (abamectin, asiaticoside, berbamine, doramectin, mobocertinib and umbralisib) were described as previously unreported OATP1B1 inhibitors.
ai_technology: Seven molecular-fingerprint machine-learning classifiers, with prospective selection by support vector classifier (SVC)
organization: Collaborations Pharmaceuticals; University of Arizona

evidence.tested: In prospective CHO-cell testing, 15 of 19 compounds predicted active by SVC models inhibited the transporter; six (abamectin, asiaticoside, berbamine, doramectin, mobocertinib and umbralisib) were described as previously unreported OATP1B1 inhibitors. The new candidate screen used contracted Eurofins assays; external execution is not a separate replication study.
evidence.unknown: The 84% refers to a small prospective test set of 19 compounds, and transporter inhibition was measured in vitro in engineered CHO cells. These findings flag possible drug–drug interaction liability; they do not show clinical interaction or patient outcome. The authors qualify six inhibitors as appearing novel at publication.
evidence.ai_role: Models trained on in-vitro OATP1B1 inhibition data ranked compounds for prospective testing. Researchers tested 19 model-selected compounds in transporter-expressing CHO cells and observed inhibition for 15, including six compounds the authors described as novel OATP1B1 inhibitors.

title: Machine-learning screening identifies natural RORγt inhibitors with preclinical psoriasis activity
summary: An ensemble machine-learning screen of natural products prioritized protoberberine alkaloids as candidate RORγt inhibitors. In vitro assays found that berberine and coptisine inhibited Th17 differentiation and directly bound RORγt by surface plasmon resonance; coptisine also showed efficacy in a preclinical mouse psoriasis model.
ai_technology: Ensemble machine-learning models for natural-product RORγt activity and counter-screening, combining graph neural networks and molecular-fingerprint random forests
organization: Bionsight; Incheon National University; Seoul National University; Kangwon National University; Ajou University; Wright State University

evidence.tested: In vitro assays found that berberine and coptisine inhibited Th17 differentiation and directly bound RORγt by surface plasmon resonance; coptisine also showed efficacy in a preclinical mouse psoriasis model.
evidence.unknown: Berberine and coptisine are known natural products; the novelty is their prioritization and experimental characterization as RORγt inhibitors in this workflow, not discovery of new chemical entities. The mouse result is preclinical and does not establish psoriasis treatment in humans. The catalog already contains an unrelated RORγt result involving topotecan; this paper's compounds and evidence are distinct.
evidence.ai_role: Ensemble models screened a natural-product library and prioritized predicted RORγt inhibitors. Chemotaxonomic analysis narrowed candidates to protoberberines; six were experimentally evaluated, and berberine/coptisine showed in-vitro effects and direct target binding, with coptisine tested in a mouse psoriasis model.

title: Machine learning reveals broad and previously uncharacterized fungal polyketide-synthase activity
summary: A genome-mining and cell-free enzyme study characterized fungal type III polyketide synthases (T3PKSs), revealing broad and varied substrate/product profiles. An ML model trained on 341 enzyme–substrate pairs predicted substrate specificity and guided tests that found two fungal enzymes, AcaePKS and PansPKS, active on all ten tested substrates, including non-natural substrates absent from training data.
ai_technology: Feedforward neural-network multilayer perceptron trained on protein-language-model embeddings and substrate fingerprints
organization: University of Groningen; University of Vienna

evidence.tested: An ML model trained on 341 enzyme–substrate pairs predicted substrate specificity and guided tests that found two fungal enzymes, AcaePKS and PansPKS, active on all ten tested substrates, including non-natural substrates absent from training data.
evidence.unknown: The enzyme products were characterized in vitro; the study examines product scope and biocatalytic potential, not native ecological roles or medical efficacy. Two candidate proteins expressed poorly, and the model's transfer accuracy was lower on non-fungal enzyme classes. The reported five enzyme sample includes only three well-expressing candidates, of which two showed the broadest tested activity.
evidence.ai_role: The model learned fungal T3PKS enzyme–substrate activity from measured data, was tested on unseen substrates, and predicted candidate promiscuous fungal enzymes. Guided experiments confirmed broad substrate activity for AcaePKS and PansPKS, including substrate pairs outside training data; cell-free assays and LC–MS characterized enzyme products.

title: CACLENS predicts and validates a zearalenone-degrading enzyme
summary: The multitask deep-learning enzyme-screening framework CACLENS selected ten candidate enzymes for zearalenone (ZEN) degradation, which were expressed and tested. One candidate degraded more than 90% of both ZEN and its analogue α-zearalenol (α-ZOL) in the reported assay.
ai_technology: CACLENS (Cross-Attention & Contrastive Learning-enabled Enzyme Selection), a multimodal multitask deep-learning enzyme classifier
organization: Shanghai Institute of Nutrition and Health, Chinese Academy of Sciences; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

evidence.tested: The multitask deep-learning enzyme-screening framework CACLENS selected ten candidate enzymes for zearalenone (ZEN) degradation, which were expressed and tested.
evidence.unknown: This is an in-vitro enzyme degradation finding; it does not establish safety of degradation products, remediation performance at environmental scale, or food/feed safety. The abstract does not name the successful enzyme or its degradation-product identity.
evidence.ai_role: CACLENS combined reaction-type classification, EC-number prediction and reaction-feasibility estimates to screen candidate enzymes. The paper then expressed and assayed ten selected enzyme candidates against ZEN; one showed >90% degradation of ZEN and α-ZOL.

title: Active learning discovers eight experimental binders for the LRRK2 WDR domain
summary: A free-energy molecular-dynamics and machine-learning active-learning workflow optimized compounds against the understudied LRRK2 WDR domain. Of 35 analogs experimentally tested, eight showed measurable binding confirmed by surface plasmon resonance and, for fluorinated compounds, an orthogonal 19F-NMR assay; measured dissociation constants ranged from 18 to 230 μM.
ai_technology: Active-learning-guided relative-binding-free-energy (AL-RBFE) workflow using molecular-dynamics thermodynamic-integration calculations and an ML affinity-prediction model
organization: Carnegie Mellon University; University of Toronto Structural Genomics Consortium; University of British Columbia; University of Ottawa and collaborators

evidence.tested: Of 35 analogs experimentally tested, eight showed measurable binding confirmed by surface plasmon resonance and, for fluorinated compounds, an orthogonal 19F-NMR assay; measured dissociation constants ranged from 18 to 230 μM.
evidence.unknown: The experiments establish ligand binding, not functional inhibition or a therapeutic effect. Confirmed Kd values (18–230 μM) indicate modest affinity, and the work is an optimization round around two previously confirmed challenge hits rather than an initial target hit discovery. This is not evidence of Parkinson’s disease efficacy.
evidence.ai_role: An iterative ML model selected ligand analogs for expensive free-energy simulations, using resulting calculations to choose compounds for further rounds and experimental validation. Of 35 procured/tested compounds, eight were confirmed as binding to LRRK2 WDR by SPR, with 19F-NMR used for orthogonal confirmation of fluorinated molecules.

title: Biological activity-profile modeling identifies SARS-CoV-2 antiviral leads
summary: NCATS researchers used biological activity-based modeling (BABM) to infer antiviral activity from compounds’ profiles across multiple assays. Of 311 model-predicted SARS-CoV-2 candidates tested in a live-virus cell-culture assay, 99 were confirmed active (32% hit rate); follow-up assays implicated viral-entry inhibition and/or autophagy modulation among confirmed compounds.
ai_technology: Biological activity-based modeling (BABM) models trained on multi-assay compound-activity profiles
organization: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, NIH; Public Health Agency of Canada; Florida State University

evidence.tested: NCATS researchers used biological activity-based modeling (BABM) to infer antiviral activity from compounds’ profiles across multiple assays.
evidence.unknown: Evidence is from cell-culture live-virus and mechanistic assays, not clinical treatment. 99/311 were active in the primary assay; further potency/secondary confirmations were available for subsets. Most confirmed compounds were reported to inhibit entry and/or modulate autophagy; these data do not establish safe or effective human therapy.
evidence.ai_role: BABM used prior activity signatures across assay panels to predict compounds with potential SARS-CoV-2 activity, including compounds outside conventional similar-structure hit finding. Researchers tested 311 model-predicted compounds in live-virus assays and conducted secondary/mechanistic assays on confirmed actives.

title: MISPOP machine learning screening identifies the oncolytic peptide Dermaseptin-S9
summary: The MISPOP ensemble screened a natural peptide library of 1,033 sequences, prioritized 16 oncolytic-peptide candidates and selected five for synthesis and testing. Dermaseptin-S9 showed membrane disruption and immunogenic-cell-death readouts in vitro and over 92% tumor-growth inhibition in a B16F10 melanoma mouse model.
ai_technology: MISPOP mechanism-informed ensemble combining XGBoost, deep neural networks and transfer learning with physicochemical priors
organization: Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine; Sichuan University; Naval Medical University; Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College

evidence.tested: The MISPOP ensemble screened a natural peptide library of 1,033 sequences, prioritized 16 oncolytic-peptide candidates and selected five for synthesis and testing.
evidence.unknown: The active peptide is a natural sequence rather than a new AI-designed molecule. Findings are preclinical: three tumor cell lines and a B16F10 mouse melanoma model (n=5 per group shown in article figures); they do not establish human efficacy or absence of toxicity beyond the tested model/doses. Only five of 16 model-prioritized candidates were synthesized and evaluated.
evidence.ai_role: The machine-learning ensemble integrated three predictors and mechanism-related physicochemical features to prioritize candidate oncolytic peptides from a natural sequence library. Five shortlisted peptides were synthesized and evaluated; Dermaseptin-S9 was tested in cell-based membrane-disruption/ICD assays and a mouse melanoma model.

title: Machine-intelligence design yields selective synthetic COX-1 inhibitors from a marine natural-product template
summary: Using Marinopyrrole A as a template, an automated design workflow generated and synthesized new natural-product-inspired molecules; target-prediction software pointed to cyclooxygenases. In biochemical assays, synthetic mimetics 2 and 2a inhibited COX-1 at 0.10 and 0.16 μM, respectively, and compound 2a was crystallographically observed bound to COX-1. Human platelet assays also showed inhibition.
ai_technology: DOGS rule-based de novo molecule construction and CATS molecular-similarity ranking, coupled with SPiDER self-organizing-map machine-learning target prediction
organization: ETH Zurich; Thomas Jefferson University; University of Bari; University of Innsbruck; Goethe University Frankfurt; Friedrich Schiller University Jena

evidence.tested: In biochemical assays, synthetic mimetics 2 and 2a inhibited COX-1 at 0.10 and 0.16 μM, respectively, and compound 2a was crystallographically observed bound to COX-1.
evidence.unknown: The study tests a small number of designed molecules; automated structure generation was rule-based and similarity-driven rather than a trained generative neural model. The COX-1 effects were biochemical/platelet assays, not clinical effects; the platelet IC50s for 2, 2a, 2b were 9, 13 and 56 nM, but COX-2 inhibition occurred at higher concentrations and selectivity varies by assay. Do not call these approved drugs or imply therapeutic benefit.
evidence.ai_role: DOGS algorithmically generated natural-product-inspired structures and suggested synthetic routes; CATS ranked candidates by pharmacophore similarity. SPiDER's cascaded self-organizing-map models predicted molecular target families, including COX. Experimental target assays confirmed the previously unrecognized COX-1 activity of selected synthetic compounds, with crystallographic confirmation for compound 2a.

title: Pinal designs functional proteins from natural-language descriptions
summary: The 16-billion-parameter Pinal model generated protein candidates from plain-language function descriptions. In four reported design tasks—fluorescent protein, PET hydrolase, alcohol dehydrogenase and metabolic H-protein—the selected designs displayed the intended function in laboratory tests; the best H-protein raised product titre 1.7-fold relative to native E. coli H-protein in a reconstituted CO2-fixation pathway.
ai_technology: Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter protein foundation model with text-to-structure (T2struct) and text-conditioned sequence design (SaProt-T) components
organization: Westlake University; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: In four reported design tasks—fluorescent protein, PET hydrolase, alcohol dehydrogenase and metabolic H-protein—the selected designs displayed the intended function in laboratory tests; the best H-protein raised product titre 1.7-fold relative to native E. coli H-protein in a reconstituted CO2-fixation pathway.
evidence.unknown: This is a primary-paper proof of concept with selected designs, not a broad hit-rate or industrial-performance demonstration. Experimental denominators vary substantially by task; extended data reports one active PETase among 94 screened and a fluorescent design selected from 29. The H-protein titre comparison was in a reconstituted pathway, not an organism or commercial process. No independent replication or therapeutic result is claimed.
evidence.ai_role: Pinal maps natural-language function descriptions to candidate protein structures and sequences. The team filtered and ranked model outputs, selected candidates for synthesis, and tested intended functions. The paper reports lab-observed fluorescence, PET-hydrolysis/esterase activity, alcohol-dehydrogenase catalysis and H-protein activity; the latter improved titre in a reconstituted multi-enzyme pathway.

title: Sequence-conditioned CogMol designs SARS-CoV-2 spike and main-protease inhibitors
summary: IBM Research and academic collaborators used the CogMol deep generative foundation model to design compounds from target protein sequence information alone for SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain and main protease. In vitro inhibition was reported for two of four synthesized candidates for each target; the most potent spike-RBD inhibitor also showed activity against multiple variants in live-virus neutralization assays.
ai_technology: CogMol, a sequence-conditioned deep generative foundation model using a molecular variational autoencoder and protein–ligand binding predictor
organization: IBM Research; Diamond Light Source; University of Oxford; Enamine Ltd.; associated research centers

evidence.tested: In vitro inhibition was reported for two of four synthesized candidates for each target; the most potent spike-RBD inhibitor also showed activity against multiple variants in live-virus neutralization assays.
evidence.unknown: The source describes a proof of concept with a small selected synthesis set from roughly 100 ranked designs. Only in-vitro target assays were performed; the leading RBD inhibitor was also tested in live-virus neutralization against variants. The paper says ADME attributes were not experimentally validated and further work is needed to confirm inhibitor binding mechanisms. These are preclinical leads, not medicines or demonstrated clinical benefit.
evidence.ai_role: The team sampled CogMol conditioned on each target's amino-acid sequence to generate candidate small molecules; candidates were filtered and ranked in silico, synthesized and assayed. The model generated compounds without target-specific fine-tuning or target-structure input at inference; assays found micromolar inhibition for 2/4 synthesized candidates for each target.

title: Prospective deep-learning screen identifies nanomolar IRAK1 inhibitor scaffolds
summary: Ro5's prospective HydraScreen structure-based deep-learning screen ranked compounds for IRAK1 and was evaluated against a 47,000-compound robotic high-throughput screen. The study reports that 23.8% of IRAK1 hits were in HydraScreen's top 1% and identifies three nanomolar scaffolds, two described in the abstract as novel IRAK1 candidates.
ai_technology: HydraScreen structure-based deep-learning virtual screening, with SpectraView knowledge-graph target evaluation
organization: Ro5 (AI Chemistry); and Strateos

evidence.tested: The study reports that 23.8% of IRAK1 hits were in HydraScreen's top 1% and identifies three nanomolar scaffolds, two described in the abstract as novel IRAK1 candidates. The new candidate experiments were conducted within the Ro5/Strateos discovery collaboration.
evidence.unknown: This is prospective early-stage hit identification, not drug development or disease efficacy. The assay validated kinase inhibition in vitro. Authors are affiliated with the companies that developed the tools. The abstract describes two scaffolds as novel candidates, while detailed similarity analysis indicates one of three nanomolar scaffolds had a similar known active; do not call all hits unprecedented.
evidence.ai_role: SpectraView selected IRAK1 as the study target; HydraScreen scored docked ligand-pose ensembles to rank compounds before prospective screening. Researchers compared rankings with automated high-throughput assay results from a 47,000-compound library and reported nanomolar IRAK1 hit scaffolds, two described as novel candidates.

title: Machine-learning prioritization and CRISPR knockout identify OsWOX13 as a rice heat-tolerance regulator
summary: Meta-transcriptomic comparison of heat-tolerant and susceptible rice genotypes yielded 409 meta-differentially expressed genes. Random-forest and XGBoost feature ranking with SHAP independently prioritized OsWOX13; CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines showed lower survival under heat stress (~20% versus ~60% in wild type) and delayed flowering, with accompanying changes in ABA, oxidative-stress markers and stress/flowering-associated proteins.
ai_technology: Random forest and XGBoost models with SHAP feature attribution
organization: Hainan University; Guizhou University; National Institute of Agricultural Science, Rural Development Administration (Republic of Korea); Pusan National University; Kookmin University

evidence.tested: Meta-transcriptomic comparison of heat-tolerant and susceptible rice genotypes yielded 409 meta-differentially expressed genes.
evidence.unknown: The PubMed primary abstract supports gene prioritization and knockout evidence, but does not establish detailed direct molecular targets or field-level yield effects. Reported survival figures concern the study's heat-stress condition and experimental lines; this is not evidence of breeding performance or resilience in field environments. Mechanistic pathway interpretations remain limited to associated physiological/proteomic measurements.
evidence.ai_role: The models prioritized stress-associated genes from meta-transcriptomic differences; OsWOX13 was among the top-ranked genes in both models. The team tested its predicted positive role using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout, followed by heat-stress survival, flowering, physiology and proteomic assays.

title: Machine learning uncovers new small-molecule chloride transporters from DrugBank
summary: After high-throughput testing 1,894 compounds and confirming 59 chloride transporters, researchers trained and evaluated machine-learning classifiers, then prioritized DrugBank compounds for wet-lab tests. Five of ten selected drugs—bazedoxifene, centhaquine, brilliant green, tamoxifen and nevanimibe—were classified by the authors as active chloride transporters, with an estimated 50–60% hit rate under their assays.
ai_technology: Machine-learning binary classifiers and consensus QSAR models trained on experimentally measured chloride-transport activity
organization: Tulane University; Rowan University

evidence.tested: After high-throughput testing 1,894 compounds and confirming 59 chloride transporters, researchers trained and evaluated machine-learning classifiers, then prioritized DrugBank compounds for wet-lab tests.
evidence.unknown: The paper combines a large primary high-throughput screen with a later ML-led DrugBank virtual screen; do not attribute all 59 initial hits to ML. The five drug-repurposing hits were measured in artificial liposome assays, not cells, animals or patients. The paper discusses assay artifacts: quinacrine/brilliant green interfere with the fluorescent assay, HCl salts can affect electrode readings, and evidence for brilliant green was weaker than for the other confirmed compounds. Authors report 5/10 active among selected candidates (or 7/12 including two known active compounds), not a generalizable clinical hit rate.
evidence.ai_role: After initial experimental discovery data were collected, machine-learning models ranked DrugBank candidates for transport activity. Researchers synthesized no new candidates for the virtual screen; instead, they tested ten prioritized available compounds in liposome chloride-transport assays. Five were classed as active; results extend these compounds' known pharmacology with membrane chloride transport activity.

title: CHOOSER uses protein foundation models to discover functional Casλ homologs
summary: The CHOOSER framework fine-tuned ESM-2 protein-language-model representations for alignment-free CRISPR-Cas discovery and pre-crRNA self-processing predictions. It nominated 11 Casλ homologs, nearly doubling the known Casλ set. Wet-lab work on selected homologs confirmed pre-crRNA processing for five of six tested proteins; EphcCasλ also cleaved target DNA and showed trans-cleavage activity, with a TTR PAM reported.
ai_technology: CHOOSER, a protein foundation-model framework fine-tuning ESM-2 representations for Cas homolog identification and Cas12 pre-crRNA-processing classification
organization: Tongji University; Zhejiang Lab; Shanghai East Hospital; collaborating Chinese research institutions

evidence.tested: Wet-lab work on selected homologs confirmed pre-crRNA processing for five of six tested proteins; EphcCasλ also cleaved target DNA and showed trans-cleavage activity, with a TTR PAM reported.
evidence.unknown: This is a specific functional genomics result, not evidence of a ready-to-use diagnostic or gene-editing tool. Only selected candidates were purified and tested; the paper reports pre-crRNA activity in five of six tested Casλ proteins and DNA-cleavage validation for a subset. EphcCasλ activity and PAM characterization are in-vitro findings. The article has a publisher-listed author correction dated 2025-01-09; this record relies on the version-of-record text and retains limited scope.
evidence.ai_role: CHOOSER mined candidate proteins adjacent to CRISPR arrays using learned sequence representations rather than alignment-only detection and prioritized Cas12 homologs by predicted pre-crRNA processing. The study reported 11 Casλ homologs and experimentally tested selected predictions; purified EphcCasλ was validated for self-processing pre-crRNA, DNA cleavage and trans-cleavage.

title: Deep learning designs selective antimicrobial peptides against Cutibacterium acnes
summary: A deep-learning design pipeline combining sequence generation and classifiers, transfer learning, pretrained protein embeddings and C. acnes-specific training data produced 42 novel peptides for testing. Five showed high-potency, selective activity against C. acnes, with MICs of 2–4 µg/mL; additional in-vitro assays tested activity against other microbes, hemolysis and keratinocyte cytotoxicity.
ai_technology: Deep-learning peptide generators and activity/selectivity classifiers using transfer learning and pretrained protein embeddings
organization: Shanghai MetaNovas Biotech; Fuzhou University; Metanovas Biotech

evidence.tested: A deep-learning design pipeline combining sequence generation and classifiers, transfer learning, pretrained protein embeddings and C. acnes-specific training data produced 42 novel peptides for testing.
evidence.unknown: All evidence is in vitro, with no animal or human testing. The 42 synthesized candidates are a selected subset of model output, and the abstract's five high-potency peptides have measured C. acnes MICs; activity against other organisms and toxicity is based on separate in-vitro assays. Do not imply topical efficacy or clinical safety.
evidence.ai_role: The models generated peptide sequences, ranked antimicrobial/hemolytic properties and incorporated C. acnes-focused training data. The team synthesized and tested 42 selected designs; five had reported C. acnes MICs of 2–4 µg/mL.

title: AMPlify prioritizes bullfrog-genome antimicrobial peptides active against priority pathogens
summary: Researchers integrated the attentive deep-learning classifier AMPlify into a genome-mining pipeline for North American bullfrog sequences. Of 101 candidate mature peptides generated from genome-annotated precursors, AMPlify predicted 75 as antimicrobial; 11 candidates were synthesized and tested, with four showing activity against tested bacteria, including a multidrug-resistant carbapenemase-producing E. coli isolate.
ai_technology: AMPlify, an attentive deep-learning antimicrobial-peptide sequence classifier
organization: Canada's Michael Smith Genome Sciences Centre, BC Cancer; University of British Columbia; University of Victoria; British Columbia Centre for Disease Control; Vancouver General Hospital; University of Washington

evidence.tested: Of 101 candidate mature peptides generated from genome-annotated precursors, AMPlify predicted 75 as antimicrobial; 11 candidates were synthesized and tested, with four showing activity against tested bacteria, including a multidrug-resistant carbapenemase-producing E. coli isolate.
evidence.unknown: This is a small selected validation set: 11 of 75 model-predicted candidates were tested and four were active. Results are in vitro and do not establish therapeutic efficacy or safety. Candidate precursor identification also used homology/genome annotation; attribute AMPlify specifically to mature-peptide prioritization, not the whole discovery workflow.
evidence.ai_role: After bioinformatics identified candidate peptide precursors from the bullfrog genome, AMPlify scored 101 mature peptide sequences and nominated putative AMPs. The team selected 11 predicted peptides for synthesis and antimicrobial susceptibility testing; four showed activity against one or more of six tested bacterial strains, including the carbapenemase-producing E. coli clinical isolate.

title: LSTM-designed peptides show antibacterial activity and mixed efficacy in a mouse sepsis model
summary: A generative long short-term-memory recurrent neural network produced 198 candidate antimicrobial peptides; five were synthesized. PEP-38 and PEP-137 inhibited carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella isolates in vitro, and PEP-137 also inhibited Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In a small mouse K. pneumoniae sepsis experiment, PEP-137 yielded 50% survival, PEP-38 did not improve survival, and the in-vitro-inactive PEP-36 control unexpectedly yielded 66.7% survival.
ai_technology: Generative long short-term memory recurrent neural network trained on antimicrobial peptide sequences
organization: Stavropol State Medical University

evidence.tested: In a small mouse K. pneumoniae sepsis experiment, PEP-137 yielded 50% survival, PEP-38 did not improve survival, and the in-vitro-inactive PEP-36 control unexpectedly yielded 66.7% survival.
evidence.unknown: Only 5/198 AI-generated peptides were synthesized. The animal experiment used one administration, small groups (12 mice per group) and a simple model; PEP-36's unexpected survival effect despite no in-vitro antibacterial activity complicates interpretation. PEP-38 did not improve survival; no mechanism, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics or safety was established. These are exploratory preclinical results, not a treatment claim.
evidence.ai_role: The LSTM RNN generated 198 peptide sequences, which were further filtered in silico; five selected candidates were synthesized and assayed. Two showed in-vitro activity against carbapenem-resistant isolates, and two were advanced into a mouse sepsis study.

title: Machine-learning-guided screening discovers potent innate immune signaling modulators
summary: At the University of Chicago, an active-learning pipeline iteratively selected molecules from a 139,998-compound library for in-vitro assays of NF-κB and interferon regulatory factor (IRF) signaling. After screening about 2% of the library, the study reported compounds suppressing NF-κB up to 15-fold or elevating NF-κB and IRF up to 5-fold and 6-fold, respectively. Follow-up cytokine assays found PME-4007 increased IFN-β secretion about threefold when co-delivered with the STING agonist cGAMP.
ai_technology: Machine-learning active-learning pipeline with variational-autoencoder molecular representations, Gaussian-process regression and Bayesian optimization
organization: University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering; University of Chicago Cellular Screening Center

evidence.tested: At the University of Chicago, an active-learning pipeline iteratively selected molecules from a 139,998-compound library for in-vitro assays of NF-κB and interferon regulatory factor (IRF) signaling.
evidence.unknown: The work reports in-vitro pathway modulation and primary-cell cytokine assays, not vaccination, immunotherapy efficacy, animal outcomes or clinical benefit. Fold changes are study-specific relative to agonist-only controls. A subset of candidates was further characterized; four tested compounds were flagged as non-viable by the cytostasis/cytotoxicity confluency mask despite strong pathway effects.
evidence.ai_role: Models were iteratively trained on screening measurements and used Bayesian optimization to select subsequent compounds for in-vitro testing. This model-guided selection led to the reported NF-κB/IRF modulators; follow-up cytokine release assays tested a subset.

title: Neural-network-guided autonomous experiments reveal an unreported TosMIC reaction
summary: A reactivity-seeking neural network coupled to an autonomous reaction platform navigated unknown chemical mixtures using real-time analytical data. Among the reactions it identified, follow-up characterization revealed an unreported photochemical reaction and a new reactivity mode for p-toluenesulfonylmethyl isocyanide (TosMIC): six equivalents of TosMIC underwent a multistep single-substrate cascade yielding a trimeric product in 47% unoptimized yield and forming five C–C bonds.
ai_technology: Reactivity-seeking neural network and junction-tree neural network integrated with an autonomous robotic synthesis and analytics platform
organization: University of Glasgow School of Chemistry

evidence.tested: Among the reactions it identified, follow-up characterization revealed an unreported photochemical reaction and a new reactivity mode for p-toluenesulfonylmethyl isocyanide (TosMIC): six equivalents of TosMIC underwent a multistep single-substrate cascade yielding a trimeric product in 47% unoptimized yield and forming five C–C bonds.
evidence.unknown: The source describes several found reactions, some previously known; this entry is limited to the distinct unreported TosMIC reactivity result. The reported 47% yield was unoptimized. The platform identified candidate reactions, while follow-up analyses and manual chemical investigation established the product and mechanism; no broad claim of fully autonomous mechanistic proof is made.
evidence.ai_role: A convolutional neural network classified reaction signatures from online NMR/IR/analytical data and a junction-tree neural network encoded reagent structures to help prioritize new experiments. The closed-loop system surfaced reactions; chemists then manually investigated and characterized selected outcomes, including the TosMIC trimer-forming cascade.

title: Machine-learning-guided optimization finds low-loading conditions for platinum-catalyzed amide reduction
summary: A machine-learning-assisted reaction-optimization study found conditions for reducing N,N-dimethylacetamide to dimethylethylamine using the known platinum complex [Pt(DMS)₂Cl₂]. The selected condition used 0.01 mol% catalyst and reached complete conversion in two hours at 39 °C without solvent, with a reported turnover frequency of 5,002 h⁻¹. The chemical catalyst identity is not claimed as new.
ai_technology: Sunthetics machine-learning reaction-optimization platform
organization: Ghent University Center for Sustainable Chemistry; Sunthetics; University of Padua

evidence.tested: The selected condition used 0.01 mol% catalyst and reached complete conversion in two hours at 39 °C without solvent, with a reported turnover frequency of 5,002 h⁻¹.
evidence.unknown: This is a single-substrate reaction-condition optimization on N,N-dimethylacetamide. [Pt(DMS)₂Cl₂] is a known complex; the reported finding is the ML-assisted optimized condition and measured performance, not discovery of a new platinum compound. The best-performing condition is reported after human-guided interpretation as well as model recommendations. The paper does not establish transferability to other amides, industrial scale-up or general performance across catalyst classes.
evidence.ai_role: The ML platform recommended reaction conditions across iterative experiments, using observed reaction outcomes to refine proposed conditions and reduce the number of trials. The team combined those recommendations with chemist interpretation and tested the predicted conditions experimentally; the source reports the optimized platinum-catalyzed reduction as a study-specific result.

title: Machine-learning and expert co-screening identifies two new silver-catalyzed cycloadditions
summary: Researchers at the Zelinsky Institute used unsupervised machine learning to filter and cluster candidate atom-economic cycloaddition reactions generated from quantum-chemical data, then used a digital co-expert and chemist review to prioritize experiments. The team experimentally confirmed two previously undescribed silver-catalyzed cycloaddition reactions yielding new products within about one week.
ai_technology: Machine-learning candidate filtering and clustering combined with the digital co-expert reaction-prioritization workflow
organization: N. D. Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry, Russian Academy of Sciences

evidence.tested: Researchers at the Zelinsky Institute used unsupervised machine learning to filter and cluster candidate atom-economic cycloaddition reactions generated from quantum-chemical data, then used a digital co-expert and chemist review to prioritize experiments.
evidence.unknown: Two reactions were confirmed from a heavily filtered set of computational candidates, with final selection and validation by chemists. The reported approximately 180-fold acceleration is a comparison for the expert-screening bottleneck, not a general chemical-discovery speedup. The abstract does not specify individual products or reaction yields; no such details are inferred here.
evidence.ai_role: Unsupervised ML filtered and clustered computationally generated reaction candidates to reduce the set for review; the digital co-expert helped prioritize candidates. Human chemists made the final selection and performed experimental validation. The source reports two newly confirmed cycloadditions; the system was a human-AI pipeline, not autonomous discovery.

title: Bayesian optimization finds mild solvent-free mechanochemical conditions for cyclopropanation and epoxidation
summary: A Bayesian-optimization-guided mechanochemical study identified conditions for the established Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky reaction using KOH in place of hazardous NaH, under air-equilibrated conditions and with no solvent or liquid-assisted grinding agent. In the chalcone benchmark, one optimized condition reached cyclopropanation completion in five minutes; the study also demonstrated cyclopropanation and epoxidation across multiple substrates, including yields of 45–75% for four additional substrates.
ai_technology: Bayesian optimization implemented with BoTorch/PyTorch, including multi-objective optimization of product yield and process mass intensity
organization: University of Parma SynCat Lab; University of Parma IMPLab

evidence.tested: A Bayesian-optimization-guided mechanochemical study identified conditions for the established Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky reaction using KOH in place of hazardous NaH, under air-equilibrated conditions and with no solvent or liquid-assisted grinding agent.
evidence.unknown: The Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky transformation itself is established chemistry; the finding is a measured, safer and faster mechanochemical process window rather than discovery of a new reaction class. A 5-minute completion time and other yields apply to the tested substrates/conditions; some prior solvent-minimized conditions could not be reproduced. The scale and substrate scope remain those reported in the paper.
evidence.ai_role: The BO models selected among six reaction variables (base identity/loading, time, milling frequency, liquid-assisted grinding agent and loading) using experimental yields and process-mass-intensity outcomes. Researchers ran the experiments, performed synthetic substrate-scope tests and used time-resolved in-situ X-ray diffraction to study milling effects.

title: Deep-learning screening identifies covalent SARS-CoV-2 main-protease inhibitor scaffolds
summary: A two-stage deep-learning screen selected cysteine-directed compounds for testing against SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease. Of 32 top-ranked compounds experimentally assayed, 12 inhibited the enzyme; six had IC₅₀ values below 12 μM, with the strongest reported at 1.4 μM. Five of those six exhibited time-dependent inhibition consistent with covalent binding.
ai_technology: Deep-learning COVCL and NOVCL classifiers integrating a directed message-passing neural network and feed-forward network
organization: Peking University BNLMS; and Peking-Tsinghua Center for Life Sciences; Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Research Unit of Drug Design Method

evidence.tested: A two-stage deep-learning screen selected cysteine-directed compounds for testing against SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease.
evidence.unknown: Evidence in the primary abstract is biochemical enzyme inhibition and inhibition-mechanism assays. It does not establish antiviral efficacy in cells/animals or clinical benefit. Potency values are for the reported enzyme assay; most tested compounds were inactive, and the six sub-12 μM hits are early leads.
evidence.ai_role: The COVCL model first prioritized cysteine-targeted covalent candidates, then NOVCL ranked those candidates for predicted 3CL-protease inhibition. Researchers tested 32 selected molecules in enzyme assays and performed follow-up tests of time-dependent inhibition for active hits.

title: AI and developmental profiling reveal conserved rules for microRNA strand selection
summary: Using a high-throughput qPCR assay, Arizona State University researchers measured microRNA 5p/3p strand use across six Caenorhabditis elegans developmental stages and selected tissues. A machine-learning model trained on experimentally measured strand usage identified compositional and structural sequence features associated with strand preference; the learned relationships predicted strand usage in other vertebrates, including humans, and the authors report that the rules are conserved but context-dependent.
ai_technology: Predictive machine-learning model using 77 biologically informed features, trained on high-throughput qPCR measurements from the HiTmiSS platform
organization: Arizona State University Biodesign Institute and School of Life Sciences; Arizona State University School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence

evidence.tested: Using a high-throughput qPCR assay, Arizona State University researchers measured microRNA 5p/3p strand use across six Caenorhabditis elegans developmental stages and selected tissues.
evidence.unknown: The dataset measured strand usage in C. elegans across six developmental stages and specific tissues; cross-species including human results are model predictions/validation against available strand-usage data, not direct tests of gene-regulatory outcomes in human cells. The result concerns strand-selection patterns and predictors, not disease causality or therapeutic efficacy.
evidence.ai_role: The model learned strand-preference relationships from the experimental strand-usage dataset, quantified feature contributions, and predicted preference across additional nematode microRNAs and vertebrate species. Experimental qPCR measurements established the C. elegans profiles; predictions across species extend the analysis but are not themselves experimental confirmation of function in each organism.

title: Biochemical-constrained generative AI yields experimentally active antimicrobial peptides against E. coli
summary: A University of Hong Kong-led team used a conditional variational autoencoder constrained by biochemical properties and a random-forest activity classifier to generate and prioritize antimicrobial peptides. In vitro testing of 54 generated peptides found 18.5% with MIC ≤10 μg/mL and 38.9% with MIC ≤50 μg/mL against the study’s E. coli model; nine peptides were classified as both active and non-toxic in the reported assays.
ai_technology: CVAE-BIO: conditional variational autoencoder with biochemical constraints and a random-forest antimicrobial-activity classifier
organization: The University of Hong Kong; University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen Hospital; Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

evidence.tested: In vitro testing of 54 generated peptides found 18.5% with MIC ≤10 μg/mL and 38.9% with MIC ≤50 μg/mL against the study’s E. coli model; nine peptides were classified as both active and non-toxic in the reported assays.
evidence.unknown: Validation is in vitro, primarily against E. coli ATCC 25922; it is not evidence of treatment efficacy in animals or humans. The reported nine active/non-toxic peptides are assay-defined candidate hits, not validated drugs. This paper generated a different peptide set and used different training/design and testing workflows from the earlier C. acnes deep-learning, bullfrog-genome AMPlify, and LSTM Klebsiella sepsis studies in this ledger; do not treat the general AMP topic as a duplicate.
evidence.ai_role: The CVAE generated peptide sequences subject to predefined biochemical constraints; the random forest ranked activity using 30 biochemical descriptors. Researchers synthesized/tested 54 generated peptides in vitro, measured MIC and hemolysis, and reported the active/non-toxic subset.

title: Machine learning prioritizes ruthenium complexes with increased MRSA antibacterial hit rates
summary: Researchers trained machine-learning models on 288 modularly synthesized ruthenium arene Schiff-base complexes and used them to prioritize 54 new compounds for antibacterial-activity testing. The model-selected set had a 53.7% hit rate against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, compared with 9.4% in the original library, an approximately 5.7-fold enrichment.
ai_technology: Machine-learning activity-prediction models trained on ruthenium arene Schiff-base complex structures and antibacterial assay data
organization: University of Bern Department of Chemistry, Biochemistry & Pharmaceutical Sciences; National University of Singapore Department of Chemistry

evidence.tested: Researchers trained machine-learning models on 288 modularly synthesized ruthenium arene Schiff-base complexes and used them to prioritize 54 new compounds for antibacterial-activity testing.
evidence.unknown: This is a study-specific in-vitro antibacterial hit-rate enrichment, not animal efficacy, clinical validation, or an approved antibiotic. The comparison is 54 model-selected compounds vs the 288-complex source library, not a randomized prospective comparison with all possible metal complexes.
evidence.ai_role: Models were trained using assay data from 288 modularly synthesized ruthenium complexes and used to predict activity for a new set of 54 compounds. Those prioritized compounds were then assessed for antibacterial activity; the paper reports higher MRSA hit-rate in the model-selected set than in the original library.

title: Machine learning discovers D-amino-acid mixtures that boost anti-biofilm antibiotic cocktails
summary: A machine-learning-guided high-throughput screen identified a five-component D-amino-acid mixture (“D-mix”) with about 78% anti-biofilm activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa at 100 μM. Combining D-mix with half the lowest effective gentamicin dose retained about 91% bacterial-growth inhibition and about 93% anti-biofilm efficacy in vitro. In a small mouse lung-infection model, gentamicin/D-mix treatment reduced measured P. aeruginosa burden by about 95% in blood and 91% in lung tissue at 72 hours.
ai_technology: High-throughput screening coupled to machine-learning regression and iterative global optimization of D-amino-acid mixture ratios
organization: University of Science and Technology Beijing Institute for Advanced Materials and Technology; National Materials Corrosion and Protection Data Center; Beijing University of Chemical Technology

evidence.tested: In a small mouse lung-infection model, gentamicin/D-mix treatment reduced measured P. aeruginosa burden by about 95% in blood and 91% in lung tissue at 72 hours.
evidence.unknown: The in-vivo experiment used a small mouse P. aeruginosa infection model, not human treatment; study-specific bacterial counts and efficacy are reported at 72 hours. The composition is a selected mixture of five D-amino acids, with authors noting the full synergism mechanism remains unclear. D-mix alone was not bactericidal under the reported in-vitro conditions; effects are combination- and assay-dependent.
evidence.ai_role: Experimental measurements of mixture biofilm effects were used to train and iteratively update ML regression models, which guided mixture selection over design rounds. The selected D-mix was then evaluated with different antibiotics in vitro; the lead gentamicin/D-mix combination was tested in a P. aeruginosa lung-infection mouse model.

title: Machine-learning-assisted screening yields an experimentally active FtsZ inhibitor candidate
summary: A fused machine-learning and virtual-screening workflow narrowed compounds from three libraries to five candidate FtsZ inhibitors for bioactivity evaluation. The compound T3995 inhibited Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 6538 and Bacillus subtilis ATCC 9732 in reported assays, with MIC values of 32 and 2 μg/mL, respectively. Morphology and FtsZ-polymerization assays supported FtsZ-related antibacterial activity.
ai_technology: ROC-guided machine-learning selection combined with virtual screening, clustering and binding-model analysis
organization: Jiangxi Provincial Key Laboratory of Drug Design and Evaluation, Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University; Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine Cancer Research Center

evidence.tested: The compound T3995 inhibited Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 6538 and Bacillus subtilis ATCC 9732 in reported assays, with MIC values of 32 and 2 μg/mL, respectively.
evidence.unknown: Evidence is early in-vitro antibacterial activity and indirect support for an FtsZ-related mechanism; the abstract does not report direct target-binding measurements or in-vivo efficacy. Hemolysis was reported as safe at or below 16 μg/mL, while the MIC against S. aureus was 32 μg/mL, so this does not establish a therapeutic safety margin. The paper’s 2025 issue date follows its 2024 online publication date; the source-publication date here is the documented first online publication (23 July 2024).
evidence.ai_role: ROC-guided ML filtered candidates from three libraries; virtual screening of acquired compounds followed, then clustering and binding-model analysis prioritized five hits. Researchers performed growth, time-kill, cell-morphology, FtsZ-polymerization and hemolysis assays, including testing T3995.

title: AI-guided HuJ3 mutation improves HIV-1 gp120 binding and neutralization in assays
summary: The IsAb2.0 workflow, combining AlphaFold-Multimer complex modeling with FlexddG mutation scoring, proposed five substitutions to improve the binding of humanized J3 nanobody HuJ3 to HIV-1 gp120. Of these, E44R experimentally improved binding (ELISA EC50 1.696 nM) and neutralization relative to HuJ3; the other proposed substitutions did not consistently improve binding, and T99R failed to express. The gain did not restore neutralization to the parental llama J3 level.
ai_technology: IsAb2.0 antibody-design protocol integrating AlphaFold-Multimer 2.3/3.0, SnugDock, alanine scanning and FlexddG
organization: University of Pittsburgh School of Pharmacy; University of Pittsburgh Center for Antibody Therapeutics; University of Pittsburgh Center for AIDS Research

evidence.tested: Of these, E44R experimentally improved binding (ELISA EC50 1.696 nM) and neutralization relative to HuJ3; the other proposed substitutions did not consistently improve binding, and T99R failed to express.
evidence.unknown: This is a single, previously known J3 nanobody humanization/optimization case, not de novo antibody discovery, animal efficacy or clinical evidence. Only one of five proposed mutants improved binding; several predictions failed and the authors note limitations in prediction accuracy and manual steps. E44R remained less potent than parental J3.
evidence.ai_role: The protocol modeled the HuJ3–gp120 complex, nominated interface hotspots and computationally ranked five single-residue mutations. Researchers synthesized/tested variants in binding and HIV-1 neutralization assays; the measured E44R improvement is the experimental outcome, while most predictions did not improve performance.

title: Generative machine learning nominates a chiral ligand validated in asymmetric C–H activation
summary: A transfer-learned chemical language model generated novel chiral amino-acid ligands for palladium-catalyzed asymmetric β-C(sp³)–H activation, while an ensemble of 30 fine-tuned deep-learning regressors predicted reaction enantioselectivity. From 490 generated ligand candidates, mechanistic and synthetic filters retained 73; the authors tested selected reactions prospectively without disclosing the model-predicted enantioselectivity to the experimentalists. One highlighted reaction using generated ligand L5 gave 94% ee, matching the model prediction of 94%.
ai_technology: Transfer-learned ULMFiT chemical language model (FnG) for ligand generation and a 30-model deep-learning ensemble (EnP) for enantioselectivity prediction
organization: Indian Institute of Technology Bombay; Scripps Research

evidence.tested: From 490 generated ligand candidates, mechanistic and synthetic filters retained 73; the authors tested selected reactions prospectively without disclosing the model-predicted enantioselectivity to the experimentalists. The coauthor collaboration tested newly generated candidates; blinding experimentalists to model predictions is distinct from independent follow-up replication.
evidence.unknown: The accepted manuscript reports proof-of-concept prospective chemistry rather than a broadly validated catalyst family: only a small, expert-selected subset was tested and the authors report that some generated ligands were infeasible or failed to form product. The highlighted result is a ligand for an established C–H activation reaction, not a new reaction class; it does not establish scale-up or utility beyond tested conditions. The selected reaction gave 94% ee, but the accessible text table names it L5 and summarizes substrate/coupling partner graphically rather than in searchable prose.
evidence.ai_role: FnG generated candidate chiral ligands from a model fine-tuned on known ligands, while EnP ranked reactions formed by pairing generated ligands with known substrates/coupling partners. The researchers selected a small set for blinded prospective wet-lab testing; the paper reports one highlighted new ligand/reaction at 94% ee, matching prediction.

title: Generative antibody language model yields a pseudovirus-neutralizing XBB spike binder
summary: Tencent AI Lab and collaborators developed PALM-H3, a pretrained antibody language model that generates heavy-chain CDRH3 sequences, and A2binder to rank antigen-antibody binding. For SARS-CoV-2 XBB, which the paper says was not present during training, the selected generated antibody (Artificial 1) bound spike and neutralized pseudovirus in vitro, with reported KD 0.13 nM and IC50 0.00301 μg/mL. The study also assayed generated antibodies against wild-type, Alpha and Delta; performance varied by antibody and variant.
ai_technology: PALM-H3 pretrained antibody generative language model and A2binder antigen-antibody affinity predictor
organization: Tencent AI Lab; Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School; Xijing Hospital of Digestive Diseases, Fourth Military Medical University

evidence.tested: For SARS-CoV-2 XBB, which the paper says was not present during training, the selected generated antibody (Artificial 1) bound spike and neutralized pseudovirus in vitro, with reported KD 0.13 nM and IC50 0.00301 μg/mL.
evidence.unknown: The functional evidence is in vitro, using SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus rather than live-virus or clinical outcomes. The study tested selected antibody candidates; several generated candidates performed substantially worse, so the reported top result is not representative of all generated sequences. The stated novelty is experimental neutralization against the XBB variant by a generated antibody, not proof of a treatment or protection in people.
evidence.ai_role: PALM-H3 generated CDRH3 sequences conditioned on antigen specificity using a RoFormer-based antibody model; A2binder scored antibody-antigen pairs to select candidates for binding, surface-plasmon-resonance and pseudovirus neutralization tests. The paper reports it generated and selected an XBB spike-binding antibody despite XBB being absent from its training set.

title: PROBY screening uncovers target-selective fluorescent probes for tau, BCL-2 and TDP-43
summary: The PROBY deep-learning pipeline screened 26,416 target-validated molecules for useful optical properties, identified 11 candidates for testing and found target-responsive probes PE859 (tau), obatoclax (BCL-2) and B3 (TDP-43). The study reports selectivity assays, cell/tissue labeling and ex-vivo tumor imaging with obatoclax. AI-guided structural modification of PE859 yielded 859-2, which enabled in-vivo two-photon and cleared-brain imaging of tau pathology in P301S transgenic mice; its measured tau-aggregate dissociation constant was 54.8 nM.
ai_technology: PROBY two-stage message-passing neural network pipeline (PROBY-L1 fluorescence classification and PROBY-L2 photophysical-property prediction)
organization: Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University; Stanford University School of Medicine; Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital; Sichuan University; South-Central Minzu University

evidence.tested: The PROBY deep-learning pipeline screened 26,416 target-validated molecules for useful optical properties, identified 11 candidates for testing and found target-responsive probes PE859 (tau), obatoclax (BCL-2) and B3 (TDP-43).
evidence.unknown: The PROBY hits are repurposed molecules from a target-validated library, not newly synthesized compounds. Target/probe performance is assay-specific; tau in-vivo imaging was demonstrated in a small transgenic-mouse study (n=3), not humans. This entry describes probe function and imaging results, not treatment effects or diagnostic performance in patients.
evidence.ai_role: PROBY ranked target-validated compounds by predicted fluorescence and seven optical properties, enabling selection and experimental verification of target-specific probes; the team then used AI-predicted structural modification alongside synthesis and bioassays to optimize PE859 into 859-1/859-2.

title: CycleRFdiffusion-designed TP4 is a reproducible cyclic peptide binder to TREM2
summary: A structure-conditioned workflow combining CycleRFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN and HighFold generated and screened 1,500 cyclic peptide–TREM2 complexes and prioritized four candidates. The lead TP4 showed weak but reproducible TREM2 binding in spectral-shift, microscale-thermophoresis and surface-plasmon-resonance assays. The authors report favorable plasma stability and moderate metabolic stability, presenting the work as an initial proof of concept for TREM2-targeted cyclic binders.
ai_technology: CycleRFdiffusion backbone design, ProteinMPNN sequence design and HighFold structural prediction/screening
organization: Weill Cornell Medicine; Macao Polytechnic University; University of Gdańsk

evidence.tested: The lead TP4 showed weak but reproducible TREM2 binding in spectral-shift, microscale-thermophoresis and surface-plasmon-resonance assays.
evidence.unknown: The only reported lead, TP4, is described as a weak binder. The evidence is biophysical binding and stability profiling, not demonstrated modulation of TREM2 signaling, microglial function, disease pathology or therapeutic efficacy. Treat this as proof-of-concept binder discovery.
evidence.ai_role: The AI pipeline generated and ranked 1,500 candidate cyclic peptide–TREM2 complexes based on structure, sequence and predicted energetics, from which four were selected for experiments; TP4 was then assessed with multiple orthogonal binding assays.

title: AI-guided natural-product-inspired molecules inhibit two multidrug-resistance transporters
summary: Combining marine natural-product fragment mining, AI-based molecular generation and structure-guided selection, the authors designed optimized analogues Ib18 and It12 targeting the ABC transporters P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2). Both analogues reversed transporter-mediated resistance in overexpressing cells and outperformed reference inhibitors. Target-engagement assays supported transporter inhibition without expression downregulation. In xenografts, Ib18 increased mitoxantrone antitumor activity and tumor accumulation without a detected increase in systemic toxicity.
ai_technology: AI-based molecular generation integrated with marine natural-product fragment mining and structure-guided prioritization
organization: Zhejiang University of Technology; Zhejiang–Egypt Joint Laboratory on Intelligent Discovery of Marine Drugs; Zhejiang Provincial People’s Hospital; University of Pittsburgh

evidence.tested: Target-engagement assays supported transporter inhibition without expression downregulation.
evidence.unknown: The evidence is cellular and preclinical xenograft evidence, not patient efficacy or established clinical safety. The abstract reports no systemic toxicity increase in the studied xenograft setting, which should not be generalized. It does not give quantitative potency values or detailed comparator identities in the abstract.
evidence.ai_role: AI-based generation contributed candidates to a natural-product-inspired library; structure-guided prioritization selected optimized analogues for synthesis and functional tests. The authors tested Ib18 and It12 in transporter-overexpressing cells and evaluated Ib18 with mitoxantrone in xenografts.

title: LIMITS-guided peptide design yields selective anti-tuberculosis host-defense peptides
summary: The Penn State/University of Minnesota team used the Lead Informed Machine Interrogation of Therapeutic Sequences (LIMITS) workflow to train random-forest and neural-network predictors on approximately 100 host-defense peptides, using lead mutational scans and biophysical sequence features. Experimentally tested neural-network-designed MAD5.1 and MAD5.3 showed reported MICs of 5 μM against M. tuberculosis H37Rv, selectivity indices >16 against an eight-organism non-mycobacterial panel, and mammalian-cell toxicity indices >100. The study identifies peptide length as a potentially underappreciated activity determinant.
ai_technology: LIMITS (Lead Informed Machine Interrogation of Therapeutic Sequences), using random-forest and feed-forward neural-network predictors
organization: Pennsylvania State University; University of Minnesota

evidence.tested: Experimentally tested neural-network-designed MAD5.1 and MAD5.3 showed reported MICs of 5 μM against M. tuberculosis H37Rv, selectivity indices >16 against an eight-organism non-mycobacterial panel, and mammalian-cell toxicity indices >100.
evidence.unknown: This is preclinical in-vitro peptide evidence, not animal efficacy or clinical treatment. The paper reports that MAD5.3 did not produce a statistically significant reduction in H37Rv viability after seven days of culture despite its MIC and selectivity/toxicity metrics; do not generalize the headline activity to every candidate or assay. MAD2.2 was moderately hemolytic. The 5 μM H37Rv MIC and high indices apply to selected peptides and stated assay conditions.
evidence.ai_role: Lead-candidate mutational scanning informed feature selection and training on a limited ~100-peptide dataset; the models iteratively selected candidate anti-TB peptide sequences for synthesis and bacteriological testing. NN-predicted MAD5 sequences were assayed against virulent and avirulent M. tuberculosis strains and counter-screened against other bacteria and mammalian cells.

title: AI generates compounds with experimentally validated pancreatic cancer cell selectivity
summary: The IRB Barcelona team trained cell-line cytotoxicity predictors on data from more than 11,000 compounds assayed across pancreatic-cancer and control cell lines, then integrated the models with a reinforcement-learning generative system to design molecules for cell-selective effects. In follow-up tests, 45 AI-designed molecules or close analogues were assayed; 20 showed the intended cell-specific cytotoxicity, and dose-response testing confirmed 18 of those 20. Across the seven selectivity exercises, at least one hit was found in five; measured IC50 values could be calculated for 12 confirmed hits and ranged from 0.97 to 16.6 μM in the targeted cell lines.
ai_technology: Cell-line-specific cytotoxicity prediction models coupled to a reinforcement-learning molecular generator (REINVENT-based workflow)
organization: Institute for Research in Biomedicine (IRB Barcelona), The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology; ICREA

evidence.tested: The IRB Barcelona team trained cell-line cytotoxicity predictors on data from more than 11,000 compounds assayed across pancreatic-cancer and control cell lines, then integrated the models with a reinforcement-learning generative system to design molecules for cell-selective effects.
evidence.unknown: This is a proof-of-concept hit-discovery study using in-vitro cell-line assays, not evidence of tumor selectivity in patients or an animal efficacy result. Only binary cytotoxicity labels at 10 μM informed the predictors; 45 generated structures or close analogues were tested, with 20 showing desired phenotypes and 18 confirming in dose-response assays. Exact generated structures were not always the synthesized compounds, and measured IC50 spans 0.97–16.6 μM for 12 of the confirmed hits. The paper explicitly characterizes this as an early hit-discovery stage.
evidence.ai_role: The authors trained predictive models on phenotypic screening data from >11,000 compounds, then used their scores as rewards/objectives in a generative workflow to propose molecules intended to kill one pancreatic-cancer cell line while sparing another or control cells. Candidate molecules or close purchasable analogues were experimentally tested and dose-response validated.

title: Machine learning generates active daunomycin-binding synthetic nucleic-acid polymers outside selected sequence families
summary: The study combined in-vitro selection with a conditional variational autoencoder trained on selection data to generate high-affinity highly functionalized nucleic-acid polymer (HFNAP) sequences. Experimentally generated CVAE sequences bound daunomycin with reported dissociation constants of 9–26 nM despite having no apparent primary-sequence similarity to experimentally selected polymers; competition selections found selected generated variants performed as well as or better than sequences obtained after multiple rounds of high-stringency selection.
ai_technology: Conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) trained on in-vitro selection-derived HFNAP sequence/fitness data
organization: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; Harvard University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Brigham and Women's Hospital

evidence.tested: Experimentally generated CVAE sequences bound daunomycin with reported dissociation constants of 9–26 nM despite having no apparent primary-sequence similarity to experimentally selected polymers; competition selections found selected generated variants performed as well as or better than sequences obtained after multiple rounds of high-stringency selection.
evidence.unknown: The finding is target binding by synthetic HFNAPs, not therapeutic efficacy or cellular activity. Binding results are specific to daunomycin and reported assays; the authors describe sequences as having no apparent similarity rather than proving wholly unrelated functional mechanisms. Some competition performance was assessed by in-vitro selection rather than a clinical or organism-level test.
evidence.ai_role: The authors used the CVAE to condition generation of novel HFNAP sequences on predicted daunomycin-binding fitness, then synthesized/tested generated sequences in binding and competition-selection assays. The machine-learning model generated the active sequences; wet-lab selection and competition assays established their binding activity.

title: Deep learning designs abiotic miniproteins that improve antisense-oligonucleotide nuclear delivery
summary: A generator–predictor–optimizer deep-learning workflow trained on quantitative delivery assays was used to design abiotic Mach miniproteins. Twelve selected predicted constructs were synthesized/tested; the strongest library construct improved phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PMO) delivery nearly 20-fold over unconjugated PMO in the standardized HeLa assay, while the authors describe the best designs as up to 50-fold more effective than prior polypeptide-based variants. PMO–Mach3/4 also produced dose-dependent reporter-protein restoration in skeletal muscle, diaphragm and heart in transgenic mice after a single intravenous dose.
ai_technology: Deep-learning generator–predictor–optimizer workflow: nested-LSTM sequence generator, CNN activity predictor on residue chemical fingerprints, and evolutionary optimization
organization: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; Harvard Medical School; Sarepta Therapeutics

evidence.tested: A generator–predictor–optimizer deep-learning workflow trained on quantitative delivery assays was used to design abiotic Mach miniproteins.
evidence.unknown: The paper reports improved delivery in a standardized HeLa reporter assay and transgenic mouse reporter model, not therapeutic correction of a disease. Only selected designs were synthesized (12 from hundreds of predicted sequences); mouse experiments used an EGFP reporter transgene and short seven-day follow-up. The article separately states the library's highest construct was nearly 20-fold over PMO alone and characterizes the designs as 50-fold better than previously known polypeptide variants; these denominators are not interchangeable. Safety evidence is limited to reported assays/doses and short follow-up.
evidence.ai_role: The model generated seed cell-penetrating sequences, predicted quantitative nuclear-delivery activity from peptide fingerprints, and iteratively optimized sequences for higher predicted activity subject to length, charge, similarity and solubility constraints. The team synthesized and experimentally assayed selected model-designed peptides; this linked the AI design to measured enhanced PMO delivery and animal reporter results.

title: AI-accelerated virtual screening identifies small-molecule binders to KLHDC2 and Nav1.7
summary: The OpenVS platform combined target-specific neural-network active learning with RosettaVS physics-based docking to search billion-scale compound libraries. The study reported seven low-micromolar KLHDC2 degron-pocket binders and four Naᵥ1.7 VSD4 binders. KLHDC2 hit C29 competed with a degron peptide at IC50 about 2.9 μM and its predicted pose was supported by a 2.0 Å crystal structure; the strongest Naᵥ1.7 hit, Z8739902234, had IC50 1.3 μM in whole-cell electrophysiology.
ai_technology: OpenVS active-learning platform with target-specific feed-forward neural-network triage, coupled to RosettaVS physics-based docking and RosettaGenFF-VS scoring
organization: University of Washington Institute for Protein Design; and Department of Biochemistry; Howard Hughes Medical Institute; University of California, Davis; Korea Institute of Science and Technology; Sungkyunkwan University

evidence.tested: The study reported seven low-micromolar KLHDC2 degron-pocket binders and four Naᵥ1.7 VSD4 binders.
evidence.unknown: Early ligand-hit discovery only: binding/inhibition was measured in biochemical competition, biolayer interferometry and cell electrophysiology assays, not in animals or patients. The paper states further optimization is needed to improve KLHDC2 compounds toward nanomolar potency. KLHDC2 C29’s crystal structure is experimental support for one predicted binding pose; target modulation, therapeutic efficacy and safety were not established. The reported target hit rates apply to manually filtered, synthesized subsets, not the full billion-molecule library.
evidence.ai_role: The target-specific neural network used docking-labeled data to guide which molecules were prioritized for additional expensive docking over iterative multi-billion-compound screens; RosettaVS/RosettaGenFF-VS performed physics-based docking and pose/affinity scoring. The AI-guided screen nominated molecules that were synthesized and experimentally tested. Experiments confirmed KLHDC2 degron displacement and a crystal structure matching the predicted pose, plus Naᵥ1.7 binding/inhibition in patch clamp. The paper attributes discovery to the combined AI-accelerated and physics-based workflow, not to a generative model alone.

title: AI-ranked SARS-CoV-2 protein interactions guide discovery of an NSP10–NSP16 inhibitor
summary: A machine-learning classifier applied to quantitative PPI assay data and AlphaFold-Multimer predictions to prioritize SARS-CoV-2 protein interactions; 15 of 34 high-confidence interactions were not previously listed in IMEx. The team then targeted the NSP10–NSP16 methyltransferase interface in an ultra-large virtual screen. Compound 459 bound NSP10 (MST affinity about 13 μM), reduced NSP10–NSP16 interaction in cells (BRET IC50 9.2 μM), inhibited complex methyltransferase activity by about 50% at 100 μM, and reduced SARS-CoV-2 reporter replication in cells (IC50 39.5 μM).
ai_technology: Multi-adaptive support-vector-machine (maSVM) classifier for quantitative protein–protein interaction data, coupled with AlphaFold-Multimer complex prediction; VirtualFlow/QuickVina2 and later docking methods performed compound screening
organization: Max Delbrück Center for Molecular Medicine; University of Luxembourg; University of California, San Francisco; Harvard Medical School; University of California, San Diego; University of Toronto; University of Cambridge; University of Antwerp and collaborators

evidence.tested: A machine-learning classifier applied to quantitative PPI assay data and AlphaFold-Multimer predictions to prioritize SARS-CoV-2 protein interactions; 15 of 34 high-confidence interactions were not previously listed in IMEx.
evidence.unknown: The paper reports an experimental small-molecule hit, not a drug or clinical effect. Compound 459 has micromolar affinity and cellular antiviral IC50; authors explicitly state it requires extensive optimization. Methyltransferase inhibition was about 50% at 100 μM in one initial assay; subsequent data include cellular interaction and reporter-replication experiments. The NSP10–NSP16 interface was previously known and had prior virtual screening, but this paper reports a different compound scaffold and tested outcomes; shared target does not make this a duplicate. In vitro and cell assays do not demonstrate efficacy in animals or people.
evidence.ai_role: The maSVM algorithm prioritized PPI interactions using quantitative LuTHy binary-assay data and AlphaFold-Multimer predictions, supporting selection and mapping of SARS-CoV-2 interactions, including the NSP10–NSP16 interface and interface hot spots. The drug-like compound hit itself was identified by VirtualFlow and docking against the selected interface, not generated by the classifier. Compound 459 was then experimentally tested for protein binding, interaction disruption, methyltransferase activity and viral replication.

title: Transcriptome-based machine learning reveals an MCL1 dependency in alveolar soft part sarcoma
summary: A support-vector-regression model trained to infer gene dependencies from RNA-sequencing profiles predicted selective MCL1 dependence in alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS), distinct from TFE3-translocation renal cell carcinoma. The authors tested the prediction with CRISPR knockout and the MCL1 inhibitor murizatoclax in two ASPS cell lines; the reported viability effects were greater in ASPS than comparator tRCC lines.
ai_technology: Transcriptome-based support-vector regression model (RBF kernel; 657 highly predictable gene dependencies)
organization: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard

evidence.tested: The authors tested the prediction with CRISPR knockout and the MCL1 inhibitor murizatoclax in two ASPS cell lines; the reported viability effects were greater in ASPS than comparator tRCC lines.
evidence.unknown: bioRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed as stated by PMC. Validation was in two ASPS cell lines with CRISPR and inhibitor assays; it does not establish patient benefit or clinical efficacy. The model nominates dependencies and is not a functional screen itself.
evidence.ai_role: The model predicted per-gene dependency scores from tumor/cell-line expression profiles and prioritized selective vulnerabilities. The study then tested MCL1 dependence in ASPS using three distinct sgRNAs and murizatoclax; those experiments, rather than the prediction alone, provide the reported validation.

title: ProT-VAE designs synthetic enzymes with measured activity and high-temperature stability
summary: The transformer–variational-autoencoder ProT-VAE generated synthetic enzyme sequences that were tested experimentally. Among 190 designed human phenylalanine-hydroxylase sequences, 69 had measurable activity and 19 exceeded wild-type activity, with the best at 2.5× wild type. A designed γ-carbonic anhydrase had a measured melting temperature of 116 °C (61 °C above the most thermostable sequence previously reported by the authors) and remained active in 23% methyl diethanolamine at pH 11.25 and 93 °C.
ai_technology: Protein Transformer Variational AutoEncoder (ProT-VAE), using ProtT5nv transformer representations and a family-specific variational autoencoder
organization: Evozyne; NVIDIA

evidence.tested: The transformer–variational-autoencoder ProT-VAE generated synthetic enzyme sequences that were tested experimentally.
evidence.unknown: The reported outcomes are laboratory expression/activity/stability tests on selected synthetic sequences; most generated candidates were not active or did not express.
